(= he looks older than he is)\nThe town centre wasn’t as crowded as usual.  (= it is usually more crowded)\nLisa didn’t do as well in the exam as she had hoped. (= you know more people than me)\n‘How much was it?  Fift y dollars?’ \n‘No, not as much as that.’  (= less than fift y dollars)\nYou can also say not so … (as):\nIt’s not warm, but it’s not so cold as yesterday.  (= it’s not as cold as …)\nLess than is similar to not as … as:\nI spent less money than you.  (= I didn’t spend as much money as you)\nThe city centre was less crowded than usual.  (= it wasn’t as crowded as usual)\nI play tennis less than I used to.  (= I don’t play as much as I used to)\nUnit\n107\nSARAH\nJOE\nDAVID\nSarah, Joe and David are all very rich.\nSarah has $20 million, Joe has $15 million\nand David has $10 million.  So:\nJoe is rich.\nHe is richer than David.\nBut he isn’t as rich as Sarah.\n(= Sarah is richer than he is)\nWe also use as … as (but not so … as) in positive sentences and in questions:\nI’m sorry I’m late. In general, we use -est for short words and most … for\nlonger words. \n long → longest  \nhot → hottest \neasy → easiest \nhard → hardest\nbut    most famous \nmost boring \nmost enjoyable  \nmost difficult\nA few superlative forms are irregular:\ngood → best \nbad → worst \nfar → furthest or farthest\nThe rules are the same as those for the comparative – see Unit 105.\nFor spelling, see Appendix 6.\nUnit\n108\nWhat is the longest river in the world?\nWhat was the most enjoyable holiday you’ve ever had?\nLongest and most enjoyable are superlative forms.\nWe normally use the (or my/your etc.) with a superlative:\nYesterday was the hottest day of the year.\nThe Louvre in Paris is one of the most famous museums in the world.\nShe is really nice – one of the nicest people I know.\nWhat’s the best movie you’ve ever seen, and what’s the worst?\nHow old is your youngest child?\nCompare the superlative and the comparative:\nThis hotel is the cheapest in town. +    "title": "A",
+    "theory_raw": "A\nstill \nany more \nyet \nalready\nWe use still to say that a situation or action is continuing.  It hasn’t changed or stopped:\nIt’s ten o’clock and Joe is still in bed.\nWhen I went to bed, Chris was still working.\nDo you still want to go away or have you changed your mind?\nStill also means ‘in spite of this’.  For example:\nHe has everything he needs, but he’s still unhappy.\nStill usually goes in the middle of the sentence with the verb.  See Unit 110.\nUnit\n111\nWe use not … any more or not … any longer to say that a situation has changed. \nAny more and any longer go at the end of a sentence:\nLucy doesn’t work here any more.  She left last month.    or \nLucy doesn’t work here any longer.\n We used to be good friends, but we aren’t any more.    or    … we aren’t any longer.\nYou can write any more (2 words) or anymore (1 word).\nYou can also use no longer.  No longer goes in the middle of the sentence:\n Lucy no longer works here.\nWe do not normally use no more in this way:\nWe are no longer friends. (not we are no more friends)\nCompare still and not … any more:\nSally still works here, but Lucy doesn’t work here any more.\nB\nWe use already to say that something happened sooner than expected. \n‘What time is Sue leaving?’ \n‘She has already left.’ (= sooner than you expected)\nShall I tell Joe what happened or does he already know?\nI’ve just had lunch and I’m already hungry.\nAlready usually goes in the middle of a sentence (see Unit 110) or at the end:\nShe’s already left.   or   She’s left already.\nD\nWe use yet mainly in negative sentences (He isn’t here yet) and questions (Is he here yet?). \nYet (= until now) shows that the speaker expects something to happen.\nYet usually goes at the end of a sentence:\nIt’s 10 o’clock and Joe isn’t here yet.\nHave you decided what to do yet?\n‘Where are you going on holiday?’ \n‘We don’t know yet.’\nWe often use yet with the present perfect (‘Have you decided … yet?’). But still … not shows a stronger feeling of surprise or\nimpatience.  Compare:\nI sent him an invitation last week.  He hasn’t replied yet. (but I expect he will reply soon)\nI sent him an invitation weeks ago and he still hasn’t replied. +    "theory_raw": "Verbs + about/of (think/hear etc.) ➜ Unit 134\nOther verbs + for ➜ Unit 135B\nA\nVerb + preposition 2   about/for/of/after\nverb + about\nUnit\n133\ntalk / read / know ABOUT … \nWe talked about a lot of things at the meeting.\ndo something/nothing ABOUT something = do something/nothing to improve a situation\nIf you’re worried about the problem, you should do something about it.\napply (TO a company etc.) FOR a job etc.\nI think you could do this job.  Why don’t you apply for it?\nsearch (a person / a place / a bag etc.) FOR …\nI’ve searched the house for my keys, but I still can’t find them.\nlook FOR … = search for, try to find\nI’ve lost my keys.  Can you help me to look for them?\nleave (a place) FOR another place\nI haven’t seen her since she left (home) for work. (not left to work)\nhave a discussion ABOUT something\n We had a discussion about what we should do.\nBut we say ‘discuss something’ (no preposition):\nWe discussed what we should do. (not discussed about)\nask (somebody) FOR …\n I sent an email to the company asking them for more information about the job.\nBut we say ‘ask somebody the way / the time’ etc. (no preposition):\nI asked somebody the way to the station.\ncare FOR somebody = take care of them, keep them safe\n Alan is 85 and lives alone.  He needs somebody to care for him.\nI don’t care FOR something = I don’t like it\nI don’t care for hot weather. (= I don’t like …)\ncare ABOUT … = think that somebody/something is important\n He’s very selfish.  He doesn’t care about other people.\ncare what/where/how … etc. (without about)\nYou can do what you like.  I don’t care what you do.\nverb + for\nB\ntake care of, care for and care about\nC\nlook for and look after\nD\nwait FOR somebody, wait FOR something (to happen)\nDon’t wait for me.  I’ll join you later.\nI’m not going out yet.  I’m waiting for the rain to stop.\ntake care OF … = look after, keep safe, take responsibility for\nDon’t worry about me.  I can take care of myself.\nI’ll take care of the travel arrangements.  You don’t need to do anything.\nlook AFTER … = take care of, keep safe or in good condition\nAlan is 85 and lives alone.  He needs somebody to look after him. (not look for)\nYou can borrow this book, but please look after it.\n266\n",

+    "theory_raw": "Phrasal verbs 2–9 ➜ Units 138–145\nAmerican English ➜ Appendix 7\nA\nPhrasal verbs 1     Introduction\nWe often use verbs with:\nin\nout\non\noff\nup\ndown\naway\nback\nby\nthrough\nabout\nalong\nover\nforward\nround or around\nSo you can say look out / get on / take off / run away etc.  These are phrasal verbs.\nWe often use on/off/out etc. with verbs of movement.  For example:\nget on\ndrive off\ncome back\nturn round\nThe bus was full.  We couldn’t get on.\nA woman got into the car and drove off.\nSarah is leaving tomorrow and coming back on Saturday.\nWhen I touched him on the shoulder, he turned round.\nUnit\n137\nOften the second word (on/off/out etc.) gives a special meaning to the verb.  For example:\nbreak down\nfind out\ntake off\ngive up\nget on\nget by\nSorry I’m late.  The car broke down. (= the engine stopped working)\nI never found out who sent me the flowers. (= I never discovered)\nIt was my first flight.  I was nervous as the plane took off. (= went into the air)\nI tried many times to contact her.  In the end I gave up. (=  stopped trying)\nHow was the exam?  How did you get on? (= How did you do?)\nMy French isn’t good, but it’s enough to get by. (= enough to manage)\nFor more phrasal verbs, see Units 138–145.\nB\nSometimes a phrasal verb is followed by a preposition.  For example:\nphrasal verb\nlook up\nrun away\nkeep up\nlook forward\npreposition\nat\nfrom\nwith\nto\nWe looked up at the plane as it flew above us.\nWhy did you run away from me?\nYou’re walking too fast.  I can’t keep up with you.\nAre you looking forward to your trip?\nC\nSometimes a phrasal verb has an object.  For example:\n I turned on the light. (the light is the object)\nUsually there are two possible positions for the object.  You can say:\nI turned on the light.    or    I turned the light on.\nobject \nobject\nBut if the object is a pronoun (it/them/me/him etc.), only one position is possible:\nI turned it on. (not I turned on it)\nIn the same way, you can say:  \ntake off my shoes.\nI’m going to take my shoes off.\nbut \nThese shoes are uncomfortable.  I’m going to take them off. The action in the past has a result now: \nTom has lost his key. (= he doesn’t have it now)\nHe told me his name, but I’ve forgotten it. (= I can’t remember it now)\nSally is still here.  She hasn’t gone out. (= she is here now)\nI can’t find my bag.  Have you seen it? (= do you know where it is now?)\nCompare gone (to) and been (to):\nJames is on holiday.  He has gone to Italy. +    "title": "Present perfect continuous (I have been doing)",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nPresent perfect continuous (I have been doing)\nIt’s been raining.\nStudy this example situation:\nIs it raining?\nNo, but the ground is wet.\nIt’s been raining. (= It has been …) \nhave/has been + -ing is the present perfect continuous: \nI/we/they/you \nhave \n(= I’ve etc.)\n \nhe/she/it \nhas \n(= he’s etc.)\nbeen\ndoing\nworking \nlearning   etc.\nWe use the present perfect continuous for an activity that has recently stopped or just stopped:\nWhy are you out of breath?  Have you been running?\nPaul is very tired.  He’s been working hard.\nWhy are you so tired?  What have you been doing? \nI’ve been talking to Amanda and she agrees with me.\nWhere have you been?  I’ve been looking for you.\nhave/has been + -ing\npresent perfect continuous\nnow\nIt’s been raining for two hours.\nStudy this example situation:\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nHow long have you been learning English? (= you’re still learning English)\nBen is watching TV.  He’s been watching TV all day.\nWhere have you been?  I’ve been looking for you for the last half hour.\nChris hasn’t been feeling well recently.\nYou can use the present perfect continuous for repeated actions:\nSilvia is a very good tennis player.  She’s been playing since she was eight.\nEvery morning they meet in the same cafe.  They’ve been going there for years.\nIt began raining two hours ago and it is still raining.\nHow long has it been raining?\nIt’s been raining for two hours. (= It has been …)\nWe use the present perfect continuous in this way, especially \nwith how long, for … and since …  . +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nPresent perfect and past 1 (I have done and I did)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nStudy this example situation:\nTen minutes later:\nThe present perfect (something has happened) is a present tense.  It tells us about the situation now. \n‘Tom has lost his key’ = he doesn’t have his key now (see Unit 7). \nThe past simple (something happened) tells us only about the past.  If somebody says ‘Tom lost his key’,\nwe don’t know whether he has the key now or not.  We know only that he lost it at some time in the past.\nCompare present perfect and past simple:\nThey’ve gone away.  They’ll be back on Friday. (they are away now)\nThey went away, but I think they’re back at home now. (not They’ve gone away)\nIt has stopped raining now, so we don’t need the umbrella. (it isn’t raining now)\nIt stopped raining for a while, but now it’s raining again. (not It has stopped)\nTom is looking for his key.  He can’t find it.\nHe has lost his key. (present perfect)\nThis means that he doesn’t have his key now.\nNow Tom has found his key.  He has it now.\nHas he lost his key?  No, he has found it.\nDid he lose his key?  Yes, he did.\nHe lost his key (past simple)\nbut now he has found it. (present perfect)\nYou can use the present perfect for new or recent happenings:\nI’ve repaired the washing machine.  It’s working OK now.\n‘Hannah has had a baby!  It’s a boy.’ \n‘That’s great news.’\nUsually, you can also use the past simple:\nI repaired the washing machine.  It’s working OK now.\nUse the past simple (not the present perfect) for things that are not recent or new:\nMozart was a composer.  He wrote more than 600 pieces of music.\n \n(not has been … has written)\nMy mother grew up in Italy. (not has grown)\nCompare:\nSomebody has invented a new type of washing machine.\nWho invented the telephone? (not has invented)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nWe use the present perfect to give new information (see Unit 7).  But if we continue to talk about it, \nwe normally use the past simple:\na:  Ow!  I’ve burnt myself.\nb:  How did you do that?   (not have you done)\na:  I picked up a hot dish.   (not have picked)\na:  Look!  Somebody has spilt something on the sofa.\nb:  Well, it wasn’t me.  I didn’t do it.   (not hasn’t been … haven’t done)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nPast simple ➜ Unit 5\nPresent perfect ➜ Units 7–8\nPresent perfect and past 2 ➜ Unit 14 \nAmerican English ➜ Appendix 7\n26\n</div>",

(not have you eaten) \nI got home late last night.  I was very tired and went straight to bed. \nUse the past to ask When … ? or What time … ? :\nWhen did your friends arrive? (not have … arrived)\nWhat time did you finish work?\nCompare:\nCompare:\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nPresent perfect\nTom has lost his key.  He can’t get \ninto the house.\nIs Carla here or has she left?\nPast simple\nTom lost his key yesterday.  \nHe couldn’t get into the house.\nWhen did Carla leave?\nPresent perfect (have done)\nI’ve done a lot of work today.\nWe use the present perfect for a period of time  \nthat continues until now. There is no difference in meaning.  You can say: \nThey have a new car.    or    They’ve got a new car. \nLisa has two brothers.    or    Lisa has got two brothers.\nI have a headache.    or    I’ve got a headache.\nOur house has a small garden.    or    Our house has got a small garden.\nHe has a few problems.    or    He’s got a few problems.\nI have a driving lesson tomorrow.    or    I’ve got a driving lesson tomorrow.\nWith these meanings (possession etc.), we do not use continuous forms (I’m having etc.):\nWe’re enjoying our holiday.  We have / We’ve got a nice room in the hotel.  \n(not We’re having a nice room)\nFor the past we use had (usually without got):\nLisa had long hair when she was a child. (not Lisa had got)\nIn questions and negative sentences there are three possible forms:\n   Do you have any questions?\nor    Have you got any questions?\nor    Have you any questions? (less usual)\n   Does she have a car?\nor    Has she got a car?\nor    Has she a car? (less usual)\n   I don’t have any questions.\nor    I haven’t got any questions.\nor    I haven’t any questions. (less usual)\n   She doesn’t have a car.\nor    She hasn’t got a car.\nor    She hasn’t a car. (less usual)\nIn past questions and negative sentences, we use did/didn’t: \nDid you have a car when you were living in Paris? \nI didn’t have my phone, so I couldn’t call you. \nLisa had long hair, didn’t she? \n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nhave breakfast / have a shower / have a good time etc. \nWe also use have (but not have got) for things we do or experience. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nPresent tenses (I am doing / I do) for the future\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nPresent continuous (I am doing) with a future meaning\nI’m doing something (tomorrow etc.) = I have already decided and arranged to do it:\na: What are you doing on Saturday evening? (not What do you do)\nb: I’m going to the cinema. (not I go)\na: What time is Katherine arriving tomorrow?\nb: Half past ten.  We’re meeting her at the station.\nI’m not working tomorrow, so we can go out somewhere.\nSteve isn’t playing football next Saturday.  He’s hurt his leg.\nWe do not normally use will to talk about what we have arranged to do:\nWhat are you doing tonight? (not What will you do)\nAlex is getting married next month. (not will get)\nWe also use the present continuous for an action just before you start to do it.  This happens \nespecially with verbs of movement (go/come/leave etc.):\nI’m tired.  I’m going to bed now.  Goodnight. (not I go to bed now)\n‘Tina, are you ready yet?’ \n‘Yes, I’m coming.’ (not I come)\nThis is Ben’s diary for next week.\nHe is playing tennis on Monday aft ernoon.\nHe is going to the dentist on Tuesday morning.\nHe is meeting Kate on Friday.\nIn all these examples, Ben has already decided and\narranged to do these things.\nPresent simple (I do) with a future meaning\nWe use the present simple when we talk about timetables and programmes (for example, transport \nor cinema times):\nI have to go.  My train leaves at 11.30.\nWhat time does the film start tonight?\nThe meeting is at nine o’clock tomorrow.\nYou can use the present simple to talk about people if their plans are fixed like a timetable:\nI start my new job on Monday.\nWhat time do you finish work tomorrow?\nBut the continuous is more usual for other personal arrangements:\nWhat time are you meeting Kate tomorrow? (not do you meet)\nCompare:\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nPresent continuous\nWhat time are you arriving?\nI’m going to the cinema this evening.\nPresent simple\nWhat time does the train arrive?\nThe film starts at 8.15.\nWhen you talk about appointments, lessons, exams etc., you can use I have or I’ve got:\nI have an exam next week.    or    I’ve got an exam next week.\nI’m going to ➜ Units 20, 23\nwill ➜ Units 21–22\nPresent simple aft er when and if ➜ Unit 25\n38\n</div>",

+    "title": "could (do) and could have (done)",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\ncould (do) and could have (done)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nSometimes could is the past of can (see Unit 26):\nListen.  I can hear something. (now)\nI listened.  I could hear something. (past)\nBut could is not always past.  We also use could for possible actions now or in the future, especially to \nmake suggestions.  For example:\na: What shall we do tonight?\n \nb: We could go to the cinema.\na:  When you go to Paris next month, \nyou could stay with Sarah.\n \nb: Yes, I suppose I could.\nCan is also possible in these sentences (‘We can go to the \ncinema.’ etc.).  Could is less sure than can. \nWe also use could (not can) for actions that are not realistic.  For example:\n I’m so tired, I could sleep for a week. (not I can sleep for a week)\nCompare can and could:\nI can stay with Sarah when I go to Paris. (realistic)\nMaybe I could stay with Sarah when I go to Paris. (possible, but less sure)\nThis is a wonderful place.  I could stay here for ever. (unrealistic)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nWe also use could (not can) to say that something is possible now or in the future:\nThe story could be true, but I don’t think it is. (not can be true)\nI don’t know what time Lisa is coming.  She could get here at any time.\nCompare can and could:\nThe weather can change very quickly in the mountains. (in general)\nThe weather is nice now, but it could change later. (the weather now, not in general)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nWe use could have (done) to talk about the past.  Compare:\nI’m so tired, I could sleep for a week. (now)\nI was so tired, I could have slept for a week. (past)\nThe situation is bad, but it could be worse. (now)\nThe situation was bad, but it could have been worse. (past)\nSomething could have happened = it was possible, but did not happen:\nWhy did you stay at a hotel?  You could have stayed with me.\nDavid was lucky.  He could have hurt himself when he fell, but he’s all right.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nI couldn’t do something = it would not be possible:\nI couldn’t live in a big city.  I’d hate it. (= it wouldn’t be possible for me)\nEverything is fine right now.  Things couldn’t be better.\nFor the past we use couldn’t have … (= would not have been possible):\nWe had a really good holiday.  It couldn’t have been better.\nNote that ‘I couldn’t do something’ has two meanings:\n(1) I couldn’t = it would not be possible now, I would not be able:\nI couldn’t run ten kilometres now.  I’m not fit enough. (= I would not be able)\n(2) I couldn’t = I was not able (past)\nI couldn’t run yesterday because I’d hurt my leg. (= I was not able)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">E</h3>\ncan and could ➜ Unit 26\ncouldn’t have (done) ➜ Unit 28B\ncould and might ➜ Unit 29C\ncould I/you … ? ➜ Unit 37\ncould with if ➜ Units 38C, 39E, 40D\nModal verbs (can/will etc.) ➜ Appendix 4\nWe could go to the cinema.\nWhat shall we\ndo tonight?\n54\n</div>",

+    "title": "may and might 2",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nmay and might 2\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nWe use may and might to talk about possible actions or happenings in the future:\nI haven’t decided where to go on holiday.  I may go to Ireland. (= perhaps I will go there)\nTake an umbrella with you.  It might rain later. (= perhaps it will rain)\nThe bus isn’t always on time.  We might have to wait a few minutes.\n(= perhaps we will have to wait)\nThe negative forms are may not and might not (mightn’t):\nAmy may not go out tonight.  She isn’t feeling well. (= perhaps she will not go out)\nThere might not be enough time to discuss everything at the meeting. \n(= perhaps there will not be enough time)\nCompare:\nI’m going to buy a car. (for sure)\nI may buy a car.    or    I might buy a car. (possible)\nUsually you can use may or might.  So you can say:\nI may go to Ireland.    or    I might go to Ireland.\nJane might be able to help you.    or    Jane may be able to help you.\nBut we use might (not may) when the situation is not real:\n If they paid me better, I might work harder. (not I may work)\nThis situation (If they paid me better) is not real.  They do not pay me well, so I’m not going \nto work harder.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nCompare may/might be -ing and will be -ing:\nDon’t phone at 8.30.  I’ll be watching the football on TV.\nDon’t phone at 8.30.  I might be watching the football on TV. (= perhaps I’ll be \nwatching it)\nWe also use may/might be -ing for possible plans.  Compare:\nI’m going to Ireland soon. (for sure)\nI might be going (or I may be going) to Ireland soon. You should go to bed.\nThe government should do more to improve\nschools.\na: Should we invite Stephanie to the party?\nb: Yes, I think we should.\nThe man on the motorbike should be wearing a helmet.\nYou shouldn’t do something = it isn’t a good thing to do:\nYou shouldn’t believe everything you read in newspapers.\nWe oft en use should with I think / I don’t think / Do you think … ? :\nI think the government should do more to improve schools.\nI don’t think you should work so hard.\na: Do you think I should apply for this job? \nb: Yes, I think you should.\nShould is not as strong as must or have to:\nYou should apologise. (= it would be a good thing to do)\nYou must apologise. / You have to apologise. (= you have no alternative)\nWe use should when something is not right or what we expect: \nWhere’s Tina?  She should be here by now.\n(= she isn’t here yet, and this is not normal)\nThe price on this packet is wrong.  It should be £2.50, not £3.50.\nWe also use should to say that we expect something to happen:\nHelen has been studying hard for the exam, so she should pass. \n(= I expect her to pass)\nThere are plenty of hotels in the town.  It shouldn’t be hard to find a place to stay.\n(= I don’t expect it to be hard)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nYou should have done something = you didn’t do it, but it would have been a good thing to do:\nYou missed a great party last night.  You should have come.  Why didn’t you?\n(= you didn’t come, but it would have been good to come)\nI wonder why they’re so late.  They should have been here long ago.\nYou shouldn’t have done something = you did it, but it wasn’t a good thing to do:\nI’m feeling sick.  I shouldn’t have eaten so much. (= I ate too much)\nShe shouldn’t have been listening to our conversation.  It was private.\n(= she was listening)\nCompare should (do) and should have (done):\nYou look tired.  You should go to bed now.\nYou went to bed very late last night.  You should have gone to bed earlier.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nought to …\nYou can use ought to instead of should in the sentences on this page. \nWe say ‘ought to do’ (with to):\nDo you think I ought to apply for this job? So you can say:\nIt’s essential that everyone be here on time. (= … that everyone should be here …)\nI insisted that he apologise. (= … that he should apologise)\nWhat do you suggest we do?\nMany people are demanding that something be done about the problem.\nThis form (be/do/apologise etc.) is called the subjunctive.  It is the same as the infinitive (without to).\nYou can also use normal present and past forms:\nIt’s essential that everyone is here on time.\nI insisted that he apologised.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nWe do not use to … with suggest.  You can say:\n What do you suggest we should do?\nor \n \nWhat do you suggest we do? (but not What do you suggest us to do?)\nJane won the lottery. \n \nI suggested that she should buy a car with the money she won.\nor \n \nI suggested that she buy a car.\nor \n \nI suggested that she bought a car. You have to be up early tomorrow.\nF\nshould 1 ➜ Unit 33\nAmerican English ➜ Appendix 7\n68\n</div>",

+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nshould 1 ➜ Unit 33\nI’d better …     it’s time …\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nhad better (I’d better / you’d better etc.)\nI’d better do something = it is advisable to do it.  If I don’t do it, there will be a problem or a danger:\nI have to meet Amy in ten minutes.  I’d better go now or I’ll be late.\n‘Shall I take an umbrella?’ \n‘Yes, you’d better.  It might rain.’\nWe’d better stop for petrol soon.  The tank is almost empty.\nThe negative is I’d better not (= I had better not):\na: That jacket looks good on you.  Are you going to buy it? \nb: I’d better not.  It’s very expensive.\nYou don’t look very well.  You’d better not go out tonight.\nRemember that:\nI’d better = I had better, you’d better = you had better etc.\nI’d better phone Chris, hadn’t I?\nWe had better go now.\nHad is normally past, but we use had better for the present or future, not past.\nI’d better go now / tomorrow.\nWe say ‘I’d better do’ (not to do).\nIt might rain.  We’d better take an umbrella. (not We’d better to take)\nhad better and should\nHad better is similar to should but not exactly the same.  We use had better only for a specific situation, \nnot for things in general.  You can use should in all types of situations to give an opinion or give advice:\nIt’s late.  You’d better go.    or    You should go. (a specific situation)\nYou’re always at home.  You should go out more often. (in general – not ‘had better go’)\nAlso, with had better, there is always a danger or a problem if you don’t follow the advice. \nShould means only ‘it is a good thing to do’.  Compare:\nIt’s a great film.  You should go and see it. (but no problem if you don’t)\nThe film starts at 8.30.  You’d better go now or you’ll miss the beginning.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nit’s time …\nYou can say It’s time (for somebody) to … :\nIt’s time to go home. / It’s time for us to go home.\nBut you can also say:\n It’s late.  It’s time we went home.\nWhen we use it’s time + past (‘it’s time we went’ etc.), the meaning is present, not past:\nIt’s time they were here.  Why are they so late? (not It’s time they are here)\nIt’s time somebody did something = they should have already done it or started it.  \nWe often use this structure to criticise or to complain:\nThis situation can’t continue.  It’s time you did something about it.\nHe’s very selfish.  It’s time he realised that he isn’t the most important person in the world.\nYou can also say It’s about time … :\nJack is a great talker, but it’s about time he did something instead of just talking.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\n70\n</div>",

+    "title": "(Requests, oﬀ ers, permission and invitations)",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\ncan/could/would you … ? etc.\n(Requests, oﬀ ers, permission and invitations)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nAsking people to do things (requests)\nWe use can or could to ask people to do things:\n Can you wait a moment, please?\nor \n \nCould you wait a moment, please?\nHelen, can you do me a favour?\nExcuse me, could you tell me how to get to the bus station?\nYou can say Do you think you could … ? :\nDo you think you could take me to the airport?\n(not Do you think you can)\nCould you open the door, please?\nAsking for things\nTo ask for something, we use Can (I) have … ? / Could (I) have … ? or Can (I) get …?:\n(in a shop) \nCan I have these postcards, please?    or    Can I get these postcards, please?\n(in a restaurant) \nCould we have the menu, please?    or    Can we have the menu, please?\nMay I have … ? is also possible:\nMay I have these postcards, please?\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nAsking to do things\nWe use can I or could I to ask to do something:\n(on the phone)  Hello, can I speak to Steve, please?\n‘Could I use your phone charger?’ \n‘Sure.’\nDo you think I could borrow your bike?\nMay is also possible:\n May I ask you a question?  \nMay is more formal than can or could.\nYou can also say: \nDo you mind if I … ? \nIs it all right if I …? / Is it OK if I … ?\nDo you mind if I use your phone charger?\n‘Is it all right if I sit here?’ \n‘Yes, of course.’\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nOff ering and inviting\nYou can use Can I … ? to off er to do something:\n‘Can I help you?’    ‘No, it’s OK.  I can manage, thanks.’\n‘Can I get you some coff ee?’ \n‘That would be nice.’\nTo off er or to invite, we use Would you like … ? +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nif I had known …     I wish I had known …\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nStudy this example situation:\nLast month Gary was in hospital for a few days. +    "title": "Passive 1 (is done / was done)",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nPassive 1 (is done / was done)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nStudy this example:\nWhen we use an active verb, we say what the subject does:\nMy grandfather was a builder.  He built this house in 1981.\nIt’s a big company.  It employs two hundred people.\nWhen we use a passive verb, we say what happens to the subject:\n‘How old is this house?’ \n‘It was built in 1981.’\nTwo hundred people are employed by the company.\nThis house was built in 1981.\n‘This house was built’ is passive.\nCompare active and passive:\nSomebody built  this house\nobject\n in 1981. (active)\n  subject\nThis house\nsubject\n was built in 1981. (passive)\nWhen we use the passive, who or what causes the action is oft en unknown or unimportant:\nA lot of money was stolen in the robbery. (somebody stole it, but we don’t know who)\nIs this room cleaned every day? (does somebody clean it? – it’s not important who)\nIf we want to say who does or what causes the action, we use by:\nThis house was built by my grandfather.\nTwo hundred people are employed by the company.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nThe passive is be (is/was etc.) + past participle (done/cleaned/seen etc.):\n \n(be) done \n \n(be) cleaned \n \n(be) damaged \n \n(be) built \n \n(be) seen etc.\nThe past participle oft en ends in -ed (cleaned/damaged etc.), but many important verbs are \nirregular (built/done/stolen etc.). +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nReported speech 1 (he said that …)\nStudy this example situation:\nYou saw Paul yesterday and you want to tell somebody \nwhat he said. \nThere are two ways of doing this:\nYou can repeat Paul’s words (direct speech):\nPaul said, ‘I’m feeling ill.’\nOr you can use reported speech:\nPaul said that he was feeling ill.\nCompare: \n \ndirect \nPaul said, ‘ I\nam  \nfeeling ill.’\nreported \nPaul said that  he   was   feeling ill.\nIn writing we use these quotation \nmarks to show direct speech.\nWhen we use reported speech, the main verb of the sentence is usually past (Paul said that … /\nI told her that … etc.).  The rest of the sentence is usually past too:\nPaul said that he was feeling ill.\nI told Lisa that I didn’t have any money.\nYou can leave out that.  So you can say:\nPaul said that he was feeling ill.   or   Paul said he was feeling ill.\nIn general, the present in direct speech changes to the past in reported speech:\n \nam/is → was  \ndo/does → did  \nwill → would\n \nare → were  \nhave/has → had  \ncan → could\nwant/like/know/go etc. → wanted/liked/knew/went etc.\nSee also Unit 48A.\nCompare direct and reported speech:\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nYou met Anna. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nReported speech 2\nWe do not always change the verb in reported speech.  If the situation is still the same, it is not necessary to \nchange the verb to the past.  For example:\ndirect \nPaul said, ‘My new job is boring.’\n \nreported Paul said that his new job is boring.\n(The situation is still the same.  His job is still boring now.)\ndirect \nHelen said, ‘I want to go to Canada next year.’\n \nreported Helen told me that she wants to go to Canada next year.\n(Helen still wants to go to Canada next year.)\nYou can also change the verb to the past:\nPaul said that his new job was boring.\nHelen told me that she wanted to go to Canada next year.\nBut if the situation has changed or finished, you need to use a past verb.  Compare:\nPaul left  the room suddenly.  He said ‘I have to go.’ (direct speech)\nPaul left  the room suddenly.  He said (that) he had to go. (not has to go)\nYou need to use the past in reported speech when\nwhat was said is diff erent from what is really true. \nFor example:\nYou met Rachel a few days ago.  She said:\nHave you heard?  Joe is in hospital.\nLater that day you meet Joe in the street.  You say:\nJoe, this is a surprise.  Rachel said you were in hospital.\n \n(not ‘you are in hospital’ – it’s clear that he isn’t)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nsay and tell\nIf you say who somebody is talking to, use tell:\nRachel told me that you were in hospital.  (not Rachel said me)\nWhat did you tell the police? (not say the police)\nOtherwise use say:\nRachel said that you were in hospital.   \n(not Rachel told that …)\nWhat did you say?\nYou can ‘say something to somebody’:\nAnna said goodbye to me and left . (not Anna said me goodbye)\nWhat did you say to the police?\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nWe say ‘tell somebody to …’ and ‘ask somebody to …’ . \nCompare direct and reported speech:\ndirect \n‘Drink plenty of water,’ the doctor said to me.\n \nreported \nThe doctor told me to drink plenty of water.\ndirect \n‘Don’t work too hard,’ I said to Joe.\n \nreported \nI told Joe not to work too hard.\ndirect \n‘Can you help me, please,’ Jackie said to me.\n \nreported \nJackie asked me to help her.\nYou can also say ‘Somebody said (not) to do something’:\nPaul said not to worry about him. (not Is working Katherine)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nIn present simple questions, we use do/does:\n  you \nlive \n→ \ndo\nyou live?\n  the film \nstarts \n→ \ndoes\nthe film start?\nDo you live near here?\nWhat time does the film start?\nIn past simple questions, we use did:\n     you \nsold \n→ \ndid\nyou sell?\nthe train \nstopped → \ndid \nthe train stop?\nDid you sell your car?\n Why did the train stop?\nBut do not use do/does/did if who/what etc. is the subject of the sentence. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nAuxiliary verbs (have/do/can etc.)\nI think so / I hope so etc.\nIn these sentences there is an auxiliary verb and a main verb:\nI\nShe\nThe hotel\nWhy\nauxiliary\nhave\ncan’t\nwas\ndo you\nmain\nlost\ncome\nbuilt\nwant\nmy keys.\nto the party.\nten years ago.\nto go home?\nIn these examples have/can’t/was/do are auxiliary (= helping) verbs.\nYou can use an auxiliary verb when you don’t want to repeat something:\n‘Have you locked the door?’ \n‘Yes, I have.’ (= I have locked the door)\nGary wasn’t working, but Laura was. (= Laura was working)\nJessica could lend me the money, but she won’t. (= she won’t lend me the money)\nWe use do/does/did for the present and past simple:\n‘Do you like onions?’ \n‘Yes, I do.’ (= I like onions)\n‘Does Simon live in London?’ \n‘He did, but he doesn’t any more.’\nYou can use auxiliary verbs to deny what somebody says (= say it is not true):\n‘You’re sitting in my place.’ \n‘No, I’m not.’ (= I’m not sitting in your place)\n‘You didn’t lock the door before you left.’ \n‘Yes, I did.’ (= I locked the door)\nWe use have you? / isn’t she? / are they? etc. to show that we are interested in what somebody has said, \nor to show surprise:\n‘I’ve just seen Steven.’ \n‘Oh, have you? How is he?’\n‘Lisa isn’t very well today.’ \n‘Isn’t she? What’s wrong with her?’\n‘It rained every day during our holiday.’ \n‘Did it? What a shame!’\n‘James and Tanya are getting married.’ \n‘Are they? Really?’\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nWe use auxiliary verbs with so and neither:\n‘I’m tired.’ \n‘So am I.’ (= I’m tired too)\n‘I never read newspapers.’ \n‘Neither do I.’ (= I never read newspapers either)\nSarah can’t drive and neither can Mark.\nNote the word order after so and neither (verb before subject):\nI passed the exam and so did Paul. (not so Paul did)\nInstead of neither, you can use nor.  You can also use not … either:\n‘I don’t know.’ \n‘Neither do I.’    or    ‘Nor do I.’    or    ‘I don’t either.’\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nI think so / I suppose so etc.\nYou can say I think so / I suppose so etc. when we don’t want to repeat something:\n‘Are those people Korean?’ \n‘I think so.’ (= I think they are Korean)\n‘Is Kate working tomorrow?’ \n‘I suppose so.’ (= I suppose she is working tomorrow)\n‘Will you be at home this evening?’ \n‘I expect so.’ (= I expect I’ll be at home …)\nIn the same way we say: I hope so, I guess so and I’m afraid so.\nThe usual negative forms are:\nI think so / I expect so \n→\nI don’t think so / I don’t expect so\nI hope so / I’m afraid so \n→\nI hope not / I’m afraid not\nI guess so / I suppose so \n→\nI guess not / I suppose not\n‘Is that woman American?’ \n‘I think so. / I don’t think so.’\n‘Do you think it will rain?’ \n‘I hope so. / I hope not.’ (not I don’t hope so)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nAmerican English ➜ Appendix 7\n102\n</div>",

+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nQuestion tags (do you? isn’t it? etc.)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nStudy these examples:\nHave you? and wasn’t it? are question tags.  These are mini-questions that you can put on the end of\na sentence.  \nIn question tags, we use an auxiliary verb (have/was/will etc.).\nWe use do/does/did for the present and past simple (see Unit 51):\n‘Karen plays the piano, doesn’t she?’ \n‘Well, yes, but not very well.’\n‘You didn’t lock the door, did you?’ \n‘No, I forgot.’\nNo, I haven’t.\nYou haven’t seen\nLisa today, have you?\nNormally we use a negative question tag aft er  \n… and a positive question tag aft er a\na positive sentence:  \nnegative sentence:\n     positive sentence \nKate will be here soon,\nThere was a lot of traff ic,\nJoe should pass the exam,\nnegative tag\nwon’t she?\nwasn’t there?\nshouldn’t he?\nnegative sentence\nKate won’t be late,\nThey don’t like us,\nYou haven’t eaten yet,\npositive tag\nwill she?\ndo they?\nhave you?\nNotice the meaning of yes and no in answer to a negative sentence:\n‘You’re not going out this morning, are you?’\n+\n+\n‘Yes.’ (= Yes, I am going out)\n‘No.’  (= No, I am not going out)\n⎧\n⎨\n⎩\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nThe meaning of a question tag depends on how you say it.  If your voice goes down, you are not\nreally asking a question.  You expect the listener to agree with you:\n‘It’s a nice day, isn’t it?’ \n‘Yes, beautiful.’\n‘Paul doesn’t look well today, does he?’ \n‘No, he looks very tired.’\n‘Lisa’s very funny.  She’s got a great sense of humour, hasn’t she?’ \n‘Yes, she has.’\nBut if the voice goes up, it is a real question:\n‘You haven’t seen Kate today, have you?’ \n‘No, I haven’t.’\n(= Have you seen Kate today?)\nYou can use a negative sentence + positive tag to ask for things or information, or to ask somebody\nto do something.  The voice goes up at the end of the tag:\n‘You couldn’t do me a favour, could you?’ \n‘It depends what it is.’\n‘You don’t know where Karen is, do you?’ \n‘Sorry, I have no idea.’\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nAft er Let’s … (= Let us) the question tag is shall we:\nLet’s go for a walk, shall we? (the voice goes up)\nAft er Don’t … , the question tag is will you:\nDon’t be late, will you? (the voice goes down)\nAft er I’m … , the negative question tag is aren’t I? (= am I not?):\n‘I’m right, aren’t I?’ \n‘Yes, you are.’\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nAuxiliary verbs (have/do/can etc.) ➜ Unit 51\nYes, it was great.\nIt was a good\nfilm, wasn’t it?\n104\n</div>",

+  "58": {
+    "unit": 58,
+    "title": "Verb + -ing or to … 3 (like / would like etc.)",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nVerb + -ing or to … 3 (like / would like etc.)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nlike / love / hate\nWhen you talk about repeated actions, you can use -ing or to … after these verbs.\nSo you can say:\nDo you like getting up early?    or    Do you like to get up early?\nStephanie hates flying.    or    Stephanie hates to fly.\nI love meeting people.    or    I love to meet people.\nI don’t like being kept waiting.    or    … like to be kept waiting.\nI don’t like friends calling me at work.    or    … friends to call me at work.\nbut\n(1) We use -ing (not to …) when we talk about a situation that already exists (or existed).\nFor example:\nPaul lives in Berlin now.  He likes living there.  \n(he lives there now and he likes it)\nDo you like being a student? (you are a student – do you like it?)\nThe office I worked in was horrible.  I hated working there. (I worked there and I hated it)\n(2) There is sometimes a difference between I like to do and I like doing:\nI like doing something = I do it and I enjoy it:\nI like cleaning the kitchen. (= I enjoy it.)\nI like to do something = I choose to do it (but maybe I don’t enjoy it):\nIt’s not my favourite job, but I like to clean the kitchen as often as possible.\nNote that we use -ing (not to …) with enjoy and mind:\nI enjoy cleaning the kitchen. (not I enjoy to clean)\nI don’t mind cleaning the kitchen. (not I don’t mind to clean)\nwould like / would love / would hate / would prefer\nWould like / would love etc. are usually followed by to … :\nI’d like (= I would like) to go away for a few days.\nWhat would you like to do this evening?\nI wouldn’t like to go on holiday alone.\nI’d love to meet your family.\nWould you prefer to eat now or later?\nCompare I like and I would like (I’d like):\nI like playing tennis. / I like to play tennis. I prefer to live in the country.    or    I prefer living in the country.\nYou can say:\n prefer something\nto something else\n prefer doing something\nto doing something else\nrather than (doing) something else\n prefer to do something\nrather than (do) something else\nI prefer this coat to the other one.\nI prefer driving to travelling by train.    or\n \nI prefer driving rather than travelling by train.\nI prefer to drive rather than travel by train.\nSarah prefers to live in the country rather than in a city.\nwould prefer (I’d prefer …) \nWe use would prefer to say what somebody wants in a specific situation (not in general):\n‘Would you prefer tea or coffee?’ \n‘Coffee, please.’\nWe say ‘would prefer to do something’ (not usually would prefer doing):\n‘Shall we go by train?’ \n‘I’d prefer to drive.’ (= I would prefer …)\nI’d prefer to stay at home tonight rather than go to the cinema.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nwould rather (I’d rather …)\nI’d rather = I would rather. +    "title": "somebody does something, has something, needs something etc., or why something exists.",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nto … , for … and so that …\nWe say:\nI called the restaurant to reserve a table. \nWhat do you need to make bread?\nWe shouted to warn everybody of the danger.\nThis letter is to confirm the decisions we made at our meeting last week.\nThe president has a team of bodyguards to protect him.\nIn these examples to … (to reserve … / to make … etc.) tells us the purpose of something: why \nsomebody does something, has something, needs something etc., or why something exists.\nWe say ‘a place to park’, ‘something to eat’, ‘work to do’ etc. :\nIt’s hard to find a place to park in the city centre. (= a place where you can park)\nWould you like something to eat? (= something that you can eat)\nDo you have much work to do? (= work that you must do)\nSometimes there is a preposition (on, with etc.) after the verb:\nIs there a chair to sit on? (= a chair that I can sit on)\nI get lonely if there’s nobody to talk to.\nI need something to open this bottle with.\nWe also say money/time/chance/opportunity/energy/courage (etc.) to do something:\nThey gave us money to buy food.\nDo you have much opportunity to practise your English?\nI need a few days to think about your proposal.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nCompare for … and to …\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nfor + noun\nWe stopped for petrol.\nI had to run for the bus.\nto + verb\nWe stopped to get petrol.\nI had to run to catch the bus.\nYou can say ‘for somebody to do something’:\nThere weren’t any chairs for us to sit on, so we sat on the floor.\nWe use for (do)ing to say what something is used for:\nThis brush is for washing the dishes.\nBut we do not use for -ing to say why somebody does something:\nI went into the kitchen to wash the dishes. (not for washing)\nYou can use What … for? to ask about purpose:\nWhat is this switch for? (= what is it used for?)\nWhat did you do that for? (= why did you do that?)\nso that\nWe use so that (not to …) especially with can/could and will/would: \nShe’s learning English so that she can study in Canada.\nWe moved to London so that we could see our friends more often.\nI hurried so that I wouldn’t be late.  \n(= because I didn’t want to be late)\nYou can leave out that.  So you can say:\nI hurried so that I wouldn’t be late.    or    I hurried so I wouldn’t be late.    \n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\n128\n</div>",

+    "title": "Singular and plural",
+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nAmerican English ➜ Appendix 7\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nSometimes we use a plural noun for one thing that has two parts. (not My trousers is)\nYou can also use a pair of + these words:\nThose are nice jeans. \nor    That’s a nice pair of jeans. (not a nice jeans)\nI need some new glasses.    or    I need a new pair of glasses.\nSingular and plural\nSome nouns end in -ics, but are not usually plural.  For example:\nathletics \n \ngymnastics \n \neconomics \n \npolitics \n \nphysics \nelectronics \nmaths (= mathematics)\nGymnastics is my favourite sport. (not Gymnastics are)\nNews is not plural (see Unit 70B):\nI have some news for you.  It’s good news!  \nSome words that end in -s can be singular or plural.  For example:\nmeans \na means of transport \nmany means of transport\nseries\na TV series\ntwo TV series\nspecies \na species of fish \n200 species of fish\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nC\nSome singular nouns are often used with a plural verb.  For example:\naudience \n committee \n company \n family \n firm \n government \n staff \n team\nThese nouns are all groups of people.  We often think of them as a number of people (= they),\nnot as one thing (= it).  So we often use a plural verb:\nThe government (= they) have decided to increase taxes.\n The staff at the company (= they) are not happy with their working conditions.\nIn the same way, we often use a plural verb after the name of a company or a sports team:\nShell have increased the price of petrol.\nItaly are playing Brazil next Sunday (in a football match).\nYou can also use a singular verb (The government wants … / Shell has … etc.).\nWe use a plural verb with police:\nThe police are investigating the crime, but haven’t arrested anyone yet.\n \n(not The police is … hasn’t)\nNote that we say a police officer / a policeman / a policewoman (not a police).\nWe do not often use the plural of person (‘persons’).  We normally use people (a plural word):\nHe’s a nice person.    but    They are nice people. (not nice persons)\nMany people don’t have enough to eat. (not Many people doesn’t)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nWe think of a sum of money, a period of time, a distance etc. as one thing.  So we use a singular verb:\nFifty thousand pounds (= it) was stolen in the robbery. (not were stolen)\nThree years (= it) is a long time to be without a job. (not Three years are)\nTwo miles isn’t very far to walk.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">E</h3>\n158\n</div>",

+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\n-’s (your sister’s name) and  \nof … (the name of the book)\nWe use -’s (apostrophe + s) mostly for people or animals:\nTom’s computer isn’t working. (not the computer of Tom)\nHow old are Chris’s children?   (not the children of Chris)\nWhat’s (= What is) your sister’s name?\nWhat’s Tom’s sister’s name?\nBe careful.  Don’t step on the cat’s tail.\nYou can use -’s without a noun after it:\nThis isn’t my book.  It’s my sister’s. (= my sister’s book)\nWe do not use -’s after a long group of words.  So we say: \nmy friend’s mother  \nbut the mother of the man we met yesterday  (not the man we met yesterday’s mother)\nNote that we say a woman’s hat (= a hat for a woman), a boy’s name  (= a name for a boy),\na bird’s egg (= an egg laid by a bird) etc.\nWith a singular noun we use -’s:\nmy sister’s room  (= her room – one sister)          \nMr Carter’s house  (= his house)\nWith a plural noun (sisters, friends etc.) we put an apostrophe (’) after s:\nmy sisters’ room  (= their room – two or more sisters)\nthe Carters’ house  (= their house – Mr and Mrs Carter)\nIf a plural noun does not end in -s (for example men/women/children/people) we use -’s:\nthe men’s changing room          a children’s book  (= a book for children)\nYou can use -’s after more than one noun:\nJack and Karen’s children          Mr and Mrs Carter’s house\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nFor things, ideas etc., we normally use of:\nthe temperature of the water  (not the water’s temperature)\nthe name of the book \n the owner of the restaurant\nWe say the beginning/end/middle of … / the top/bottom of … / the front/back/side of … :\nthe beginning of the month (not the month’s beginning)\nthe top of the hill                           the back of the car\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nYou can usually use -’s or of … for an organisation (= a group of people).  So you can say:\nthe government’s decision     or     the decision of the government\nthe company’s success \n or the success of the company\nWe also use -’s for places.  So you can say:\nthe city’s streets         the world’s population         Italy’s prime minister\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nWe use -’s with time words (yesterday / next week etc.):\nDo you still have yesterday’s newspaper?\n Next week’s meeting has been cancelled.\nIn the same way, you can say today’s / tomorrow’s / this evening’s / Monday’s etc.\nWe also use -’s (or -s’ with plural words) with periods of time:\nI’ve got a week’s holiday starting on Monday.\nJulia has got three weeks’ holiday.\nI live near the station – it’s only ten minutes’ walk.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">E</h3>\nNoun + noun (a bus driver) ➜ Unit 80\na three-hour journey, a ten-pound note ➜ Unit 80E \n-’s (= is or has) in short forms ➜ Appendix 5.2\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\n162\n</div>",

We use some/somebody/something to talk about a person  \nor thing that we know exists, or we think exists:\nAre you waiting for somebody? (I think you are waiting for somebody)\nWe use some in questions when we ask for or offer things:\nCan I have some sugar, please? (there is probably some sugar that I can have)\nWould you like something to eat? (there is something to eat)\nBut in most questions, we use any. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nall / all of  most / most of  no / none of etc.\nall \n \nsome \n \nany \n \nmost \n \nmuch \n \nmany \n \n(a) littl e \n(a) few \n \nno\nYou can use these words with a noun (some food / few books etc.):\nAll cars have wheels.\nSome cars can go faster than others.\nMany people drive too fast.\nI go away most weekends.\nI feel really tired.  I’ve got no energy.\nWe do not say ‘all of cars’, ‘some of people’ etc. (see Section B):\nSome people learn more easily than others. (not Some of people)\nall  \nhalf  \nsome  \nany  \nmost  \nmuch  \nmany  \n(a) little\n(a) few\nnone\nYou can use these words with of (some of / most of etc.):\nsome of\nmost of\nnone of   etc.\n+\nthe … \nmy … \nthis … \nthese … \nthat … \nthose … etc.\nSo you can say:\nsome of the people, some of those people  (but not some of people) \n \nmost of my time, most of the time  (but not most of time)\nSome of the people I work with are very strange.\nNone of this money is mine.\nHave you read any of these books?\nI was ill yesterday.  I spent most of the day in bed.\nYou don’t need of after all or half.  So you can say:\nAll my friends live near here.    or    All of my friends …\nHalf this money is mine.    or    Half of this money …\nCompare:\nAll flowers are beautiful. (= all flowers in general)\n \nAll (of) these flowers are beautiful. (= a specific group of flowers)\nMost problems have a solution. (= most problems in general)\nWe were able to solve most of the problems we had. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nall   every   whole \neverybody/everyone/everything and all \nWe say:\nEverybody was happy.     or     Everyone was happy. (not all were happy)\nHe thinks he knows everything. (not knows all)\nOur holiday was a disaster.  Everything went wrong. (not all went wrong)\nWe do not often use all alone in this way.  We do not say ‘all were happy’, ‘he knows all’ etc.\nWe use all in the following ways:  \nall + noun (all cars, all my money etc.) \nall of + us/you/them\nwe/you/they … all … (see also Unit 110D)\nall about …\nall … = the only thing(s)\nAll my friends were happy.\nAll of us were happy.\nWe were all happy.\nHe knows all about computers.\nAll I’ve eaten today is a banana. \n(= the only thing I’ve eaten today)\nwhole and all\nWhole = complete, entire.  We use whole mostly with singular nouns:\nDid you read the whole book? (= all the book, not just a part of it)\nEmily has lived her whole life in the same town.\nI was so hungry, I ate a whole packet of biscuits. (= a complete packet)\nWe do not normally use whole with uncountable nouns (water, food, money etc.).  \nWe say:\nDid you spend all the money I gave you?   (not the whole money)\nI read all the information carefully. (not the whole information)\nWe use the/my/a etc. before whole.  Compare whole and all:\nI read the whole book.    but    I read all the information.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nevery day / all day / the whole day\nWe use every to say how often something happens (every day / every ten minutes etc.):\nWhen we were on holiday, we went to the beach every day. (not all days)\nThe bus service is excellent. He didn’t say a word all evening.    or    … the whole evening.\nNote that we say all day (not all the day), all week (not all the week) etc.\nCompare all the time and every time:\nThey never go out.  They are at home all the time. (= always, continuously)\nEvery time I see you, you look different. (= each time, on every occasion)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nEvery/everybody/everyone/everything are singular words, so we use a singular verb:\nEvery seat in the theatre was taken.\nEverybody has arrived. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nRelative clauses 1: clauses with who/that/which\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nStudy this example situation:\nLast week we had a party and a lot of people came.  Everybody enjoyed it.\n \nEverybody  who came to the party   enjoyed it.\nA clause is a part of a sentence.  A relative clause tells us which person or thing (or what kind of\nperson or thing) the speaker means:\nthe woman who lives next door to me  \n(‘who lives next door to me’ tells us which woman)\npeople who complain all the time\n(‘who complain all the time’  tells us what kind of people)\nWe use who in a relative clause for people (not things):\nThe woman who lives next door to me is a doctor.\nI don’t like people who complain all the time.\nAn architect is someone who designs buildings.\nWhat was the name of the person who called?\nDo you know anyone who wants to buy a car?\nWe also use that for people, but not which:\nThe woman that lives next door to me is a doctor. (not the woman which)\nSometimes you must use who (not that) for people – see Unit 95.\nrelative clause\nWhen we are talking about things, we use that or which (not who) in a relative clause:\nI don’t like stories that have unhappy endings. \nor    … stories which have unhappy endings. \nGrace works for a company that makes furniture. \nor    … a company which makes furniture.\nThe machine that broke down is working again now. \nor    The machine which broke down …\nIn these examples that is more usual than which, but sometimes you must use which.  See Unit 95.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nIn relative clauses we use who/that/which, not he/she/they/it. \nCompare:\nI met a Canadian woman at the party.  She is an English teacher. (2 sentences) \nI met a Canadian woman who is an English teacher. (1 sentence)\nI can’t find the keys.  They were on the table.  \nWhere are the keys that were on the table? (not the keys they were)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nWhat = the thing(s) that\nCompare what and that:\nWhat happened was my fault. (= the thing that happened)\nbut\nEverything that happened was my fault.  \n(not Everything what happened)\nThe machine that broke down is now working again. \n(not The machine what broke down)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nRelative clauses 2–5 ➜ Units 93–96\n184\n</div>",

+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nRelative clauses 2: \nclauses with and without who/that/which\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nLook at these example sentences from Unit 92:\nThe woman  who  lives next door to me is a doctor. (or The woman that lives …)\nThe woman  lives next  door to me \nwho (= the woman) is the subject\nWhere are the keys  that  were on the table? (or … the keys which were …)\nThe keys  were on the table \nthat (= the keys) is the subject\nYou must use who/that/which when it is the subject of the relative clause.  You cannot leave out\nwho/that/which in these examples.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nwho (= the woman) is the object\nI is the subject\nthat (= the keys) is the object\nyou is the subject\nSometimes who/that/which is the object of the verb.  For example:\n The woman  who  I wanted to see was away on holiday. \nI wanted to see  the woman\nDid you find the keys  that  you lost? \nyou lost  the keys\nWhen who/that/which is the object, you can leave it out.  So you can say:\nThe woman I wanted to see was away.    or    The woman who I wanted to see …\nDid you find the keys you lost?    or    … the keys that you lost?\nThe dress Lisa bought doesn’t fit her very well.    or    The dress that Lisa bought …\nIs there anything I can do?    or    … anything that I can do?\nNote that we say:\nthe keys you lost   (not the keys you lost them)\nthe dress Lisa bought   (not the dress Lisa bought it)\nNote the position of prepositions (to/in/for etc.) in relative clauses:\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nTom is  talking to  a woman.  Do you know her? (2 sentences)\nDo you know the woman Tom is  talking to ? (or … the woman who/that Tom is talking to)\nI  slept in  a bed.  It wasn’t comfortable. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nRelative clauses 3: whose/whom/where\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nwhose\nStudy this example situation:\nWhen we were driving home, we saw some people standing by the \nroad.  Their car had broken down, so we stopped to help them.\nWe helped some people whose car had broken down. \n(= their car had broken down)\nWe use whose mostly for people:\nA widow is a woman whose husband is dead. \n \n(her husband is dead)\nI met someone whose brother I went to school with. \n(I went to school with his/her brother)\nCompare who and whose:\nI met a man who knows you. (he knows you)\nI met a man whose sister knows you. (his sister knows you)\nDo not confuse whose and who’s.  The pronunciation is the same, but who’s = who is or who has:\nI have a friend who’s learning Arabic. (who’s = who is)\nI have a friend who’s just started learning Arabic. (who’s = who has)\nI have a friend whose sister is learning Arabic. \nwhom\nWhom is possible instead of who when it is the object of the verb (see Unit 93B):\nGeorge is a person whom I admire very much. (I admire him)\nYou can also use a preposition + whom (to whom / from whom / with whom etc.):\nIt’s important to have friends with whom you can relax. (you can relax with them)\nWhom is a formal word and we do not oft en use it in spoken English.  We usually prefer to say:\na person I admire a lot    or    a person who/that I admire a lot\nfriends you can relax with    or    friends who/that you can relax with \n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nwhere\nWe use where in a relative clause to talk about a place:\nI recently went back to the town where I grew up. (I grew up there)\nThe restaurant where we had lunch was near the airport.\nI would like to live in a place where there is plenty of sunshine.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nthe day, the time, the reason … \nWe say ‘the day we got married’, ‘the year I was born’, ‘the last time they met’ etc. :\nI can’t meet you on Friday.  That’s the day I’m going away.\n The last time I saw her, she looked great.\nYou can also use that:\nThe last time that I saw her, she looked great.\nWe say ‘the reason I’m calling you’, ‘the reason she didn’t get the job’ etc.\n The reason I’m calling you is to ask your advice.\nYou can also use that:\nThe reason that I’m calling you …    or    The reason why I’m calling you …\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nRelative clauses 1–2 ➜ Units 92–93\nRelative clauses 4–5 ➜ Units 95–96\nwhom ➜ Unit 96\n188\n</div>",

+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\n-ing and -ed clauses (the woman talking to Tom,\nthe boy injured in the accident)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nA clause is a part of a sentence.  Some clauses begin with -ing.  For example:\nWho is the woman talking to Tom? \nThe boy injured in the accident was taken to hospital.\n-ing clause\nTOM\nthe woman \ntalking to Tom\n-ed clause\nWe use -ing clauses to say what somebody (or something) is (or was) doing at a particular time:\nWho is the woman talking to Tom? (the woman is talking to Tom)\nPolice investigating the crime are looking for three men. (police are investigating the crime)\nWho were those people waiting outside? (they were waiting)\nI was woken up by a bell ringing. (a bell was ringing)\nYou can also use an -ing clause to say what happens all the time, not just at a particular time:\nThe road connecting the two villages is very narrow. (the road connects the two villages)\nI have a large room overlooking the garden. (the room overlooks the garden)\nCan you think of the name of a flower beginning with T? (the name begins with T)\n-ed clauses have a passive meaning:\nThe boy injured in the accident was taken to hospital.\n(he was injured in the accident)\nGeorge showed me some pictures painted by his father.\n(they were painted by his father)\nThe gun used in the robbery has been found.\n(the gun was used in the robbery)\nInjured/painted/used are past participles.  Most past participles end in -ed, but many are irregular \n(stolen/made/built etc.):\nThe police never found the money stolen in the robbery.\nMost of the goods made in this factory are exported.\nSome clauses begin with -ed (injured, painted etc.).  For example:\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nYou can use there is / there was (etc.) + -ing and -ed clauses:\nThere were some children swimming in the river.\nIs there anybody waiting?\nThere was a big red car parked outside the house.\nWe use left  in this way, with the meaning ‘not used, still there’:\nWe’ve eaten nearly all the chocolates.  There are only a few left .\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nsee/hear somebody doing something ➜ Unit 67\n-ing clauses ➜ Unit 68\nthere (is) ➜ Unit 84\nIrregular past participles (made/stolen etc.) ➜ Appendix 1\nthe boy injured \nin the accident\n194\n</div>",

They give us information about \nage, size, colour etc.\nAdjectives like nice/beautiful are opinion adjectives.  They tell us what the speaker thinks of\nsomething or somebody.\nOpinion adjectives usually go before fact adjectives.\na\nan\na\nopinion\nnice\ninteresting\ndelicious\nbeautiful\nfact\nlong\nyoung\nhot\nlarge round wooden\nsummer holiday\nman\nvegetable soup\ntable\nSometimes we use two or more fact adjectives together. +    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nAdjectives and adverbs 2\n(well, fast, late, hard/hardly)\ngood and well\nGood is an adjective.  The adverb is well:\nYour English is good. \nbut    You speak English well.\nSophie is a good pianist.    but    Sophie plays the piano well.\nWe use well (not good) with past participles (known/educated etc.).  For example:\nwell-known \n \nwell-educated \n \nwell-paid \n \nwell-behaved\nSophie’s father is a well-known writer.\nWell is also an adjective meaning ‘in good health’:\n‘How are you today?’ \n‘I’m very well, thanks.’\nAdjectives aft er verbs (‘You look tired’ etc.) ➜ Unit 99C\nAdjectives and adverbs 1 ➜ Unit 100\nfast, hard and late\nThese words are both adjectives and adverbs:\n \nadjective\nadverb\nDarren is a fast runner.  \nDarren can run fast.\nIt’s hard to find a job right now.  \nKate works hard. (not works hardly)\nSorry I’m late.  \nI got up late.\nlately = recently:\nHave you seen Kate lately?\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nhardly\nhardly = very little, almost not:\nSarah wasn’t very friendly at the party.  She hardly spoke to me.\n(= she spoke to me very little)\nWe’ve only met once or twice.  We hardly know each other.\nCompare hard and hardly:\nHe tried hard to find a job, but he had no luck.  (= he tried a lot, with a lot of eff ort)\nI’m not surprised he didn’t find a job.  He hardly tried.  (= he tried very little)\nHardly goes before the verb:\nWe hardly know each other. She’s quite famous.  or   She’s pretty famous.  \n(= less than ‘very famous’, but more than ‘a little famous’)\nAnna lives quite near me, so we see each other pretty often.\nPretty is an informal word and is used mainly in spoken English.\nQuite goes before a/an:\n We live in quite an old house. (not a quite old house)\nCompare:\nSarah has quite a good job.\nSarah has a pretty good job.\nYou can also use quite (but not pretty) in the following ways:\nquite a/an + noun (without an adjective):\n I didn’t expect to see them.  It was quite a surprise.  (= quite a big surprise)\nquite a lot (of …):\n There were quite a lot of guests at the wedding.\nquite + verb, especially like and enjoy:\nI quite like tennis, but it’s not my favourite sport.\nRather is similar to quite and pretty.  We often use rather for negative ideas (things we think are not \ngood):\nThe weather isn’t so good.  It’s rather cloudy.\n Paul is rather shy.  He doesn’t talk very much.\nQuite is also possible in these examples.\nWhen we use rather for positive ideas (good/nice etc.), it means ‘unusually’ or ‘surprisingly’:\nThese oranges are rather good.  Where did you get them?\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nFairly is weaker than quite/rather/pretty.  For example, if something is fairly good, it is not very\ngood and it could be better:\nMy room is fairly big, but I’d prefer a bigger one.\nWe see each other fairly often, but not as often as we used to.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nQuite also means ‘completely’.  For example:\n‘Are you sure?’     ‘Yes, quite sure.’  (= completely sure)\nQuite means ‘completely’ with a number of adjectives, especially:\nsure \nright \ntrue \nclear \n different \n incredible \n amazing\ncertain \nwrong \nsafe \nobvious \n unnecessary \n extraordinary \n impossible\nShe was quite different from what I expected. (= I completely agree)\nnot quite = not completely:\nI don’t quite understand what you mean.\n‘Are you ready yet?’ \n‘Not quite.’  (= not completely)\nCompare the two meanings of quite:\nThe story is quite interesting.  (= less than ‘very interesting’)\nThe story is quite true.  (= completely true)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\n208\n</div>",

+    "theory": "<div class=\"grammar-theory\" style=\"white-space: pre-wrap; font-family: sans-serif; line-height: 1.6;\">\nany/no ➜ Unit 86\nComparative 1, 3 ➜ Units 105, 107\neldest ➜ Unit 108C \neven + comparative ➜ Unit 112C\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">A</h3>\nComparative 2 (much better / any better etc.)\nmuch / a lot etc. + comparative\nBefore comparatives you can use:\nmuch \n \na lot \n \nfar (= a lot) \n \na bit \n \na little \n \nslightly (= a little)\nI felt ill earlier, but I feel much better now. (or a lot better)\nDon’t go by train.  It’s a lot more expensive. (or much more expensive)\nCould you speak a bit more slowly?   (or a little more slowly)\nThis bag is slightly heavier than the other one.\nThe problem is far more serious than we thought at first. \nany / no + comparative\nYou can use any and no + comparative (any longer / no bigger etc.):\nI’ve waited long enough. I’m not waiting any longer. (= not even a little longer)\nWe expected their apartment to be very big, but it’s no bigger than ours.  \nor    … it isn’t any bigger than ours. Do you feel any better?\nThis hotel is better than the other one, and it’s no more expensive.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">B</h3>\nbetter and better, more and more etc.\nWe repeat comparatives (better and better etc.) to say that something changes continuously:\nYour English is improving.  It’s getting better and better.\nThe city has grown fast in recent years.  It’s got bigger and bigger.\nAs I listened to his story, I became more and more convinced that he was lying.\nMore and more tourists are visiting this part of the country.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">C</h3>\nthe … the …\nYou can say the sooner the better, the more the better etc. :\na: What time shall we leave?\nB: The sooner the better. (= as soon as possible)\na: What sort of bag do you want?  A big one?\nB: Yes, the bigger the better. (= as big as possible)\nWhen you’re travelling, the less luggage you have the better.\nWe also use the … the … to say that one thing depends on another thing:\nThe sooner we leave, the earlier we’ll arrive. (= if we leave sooner, we’ll arrive earlier)\nThe younger you are, the easier it is to learn.\nThe more expensive the hotel, the better the service.\nThe more I thought about the plan, the less I liked it.\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">D</h3>\nolder and elder\nThe comparative of old is older:\nDavid looks older than he really is. (or My older sister …)\nBut we do not say that ‘somebody is elder’:\nMy sister is older than me. (not elder than me)\n<h3 class=\"text-xl font-bold mt-6 mb-2 text-primary\">E</h3>\n212\n</div>",

In general, we use -est for short words and most … for\nlonger words. \n long → longest  \nhot → hottest \neasy → easiest \nhard → hardest\nbut    most famous \nmost boring \nmost enjoyable  \nmost difficult\nA few superlative forms are irregular:\ngood → best \nbad → worst \nfar → furthest or farthest\nThe rules are the same as those for the comparative – see Unit 105.\nFor spelling, see Appendix 6.\nWhat is the longest river in the world?\nWhat was the most enjoyable holiday you’ve ever had?\nLongest and most enjoyable are superlative forms.\nWe normally use the (or my/your etc.) with a superlative:\nYesterday was the hottest day of the year.\nThe Louvre in Paris is one of the most famous museums in the world.\nShe is really nice – one of the nicest people I know.\nWhat’s the best movie you’ve ever seen, and what’s the worst?\nHow old is your youngest child?\nCompare the superlative and the comparative:\nThis hotel is the cheapest in town.
